Dowling examined the impact of saltwater and erosion on Horseshoe Bay Lagoon, a freshwater lagoon and one of the few swamps with bulkuru sedge—also known as water chestnut—on the island. The study is published in the journal Applied Sciences.

top.title: Researchers study how AI could improve weed management
top.summary: Advances in weed management technology could reduce reliance on herbicides and manual labor, but a new review from the University of Mississippi and Cornell University indicates those tools also bring steep costs and potential challenges.

top.title: Forgotten samples from Greenland's Cold War base reveal warmer summers during ancient ice-free period
top.summary: The site of a former U.S. military base in Greenland was ice-free at a time when summers were a few degrees warmer than today, according to a new University at Buffalo–led study of ancient sediment recovered from beneath the site in the 1960s.

more.title: Like humans, some primates become cautious of germs in the wake of a viral outbreak
more.summary: In the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, many households wiped down groceries with disinfectant before putting them away. Hand sanitizer was in short supply. With little information on how the virus spread, people became more cautious of germs from other people. A new University of California San Diego study suggests that humans may not be alone in changing behavior after experiencing a disease threat.

more.title: Diverse and sustained social activities may boost cognition in older age
more.summary: Diverse and sustained social activities may boost cognitive performance and slow the decline in brain health associated with aging, suggest the findings of a large international study, published online in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health.

more.title: Soybean waste yields 3D-printable material that could help repair skin
more.summary: Transforming a soybean processing byproduct into a material for skin protection and repair is the prospect outlined by a study that used okara, a residue from the production of tofu and soy-based beverages, to obtain a bioactive, biodegradable, 3D-printable biomaterial.

more.title: New study reveals the high financial value of privacy in legal proceedings
more.summary: A new Management Science study provides rare real-world evidence that people are willing to give up thousands of dollars to prevent sensitive information about their health and income from becoming public. The research, developed over five years by an international team, has now also laid the foundation for a European research project led by Ehud Guttel of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

more.title: Guatemala gains its first endemic bird in American Ornithological Society's 67th supplement
more.summary: The 67th Supplement to the American Ornithological Society's (AOS's) Check-list of North American Birds, which was published today in Ornithology, includes several significant updates to the classification of bird species found in North America, Central America and the Caribbean.

more.title: A magnetar can be born when two neutron stars touch
more.summary: All neutron stars have intense magnetic fields. The typical magnetic field of a neutron star is about 100,000 times stronger than the strongest magnetic fields we can create on Earth. But about 1% of neutron stars have even stronger magnetic fields. Known as magnetars, their magnetic fields can be 1,000 times stronger than a regular magnetic field.

more.title: Women farmers need better financing to benefit from AI
more.summary: Public and private investments must address the financial barriers preventing women from benefiting fully from digital technologies and artificial intelligence as multiple global crises and aid cuts bite.

more.title: Are partisan politics even changing up our accents? They just might be, y'all
more.summary: With the midterms fast approaching, communicating just the right message has been top of mind on all sides of the political aisle.

more.title: Controlled vapor treatment guides molecules into highly oriented soft quasicrystals
more.summary: Molecules can spontaneously organize into complex, ordered structures through a process known as self-assembly. Among these structures, soft quasicrystals display unusual patterns that do not repeat regularly like conventional crystals. However, producing such structures with a uniform orientation over large areas remains a major challenge.

more.title: Scientists finally uncover why statins can cause muscle pain
more.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why statins, the widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering drugs that help prevent heart attacks and strokes, can sometimes cause muscle pain, weakness, and even severe muscle damage. Using advanced imaging technology, researchers discovered that statins can attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells and force open a channel that normally controls calcium flow.

more.title: Hurricane warning maps are improving, but a dangerous problem remains
more.summary: A new study reveals that improved hurricane forecast graphics may help people identify threatened areas without making them more likely to recognize the danger or take protective action. Researchers also found that a widespread misunderstanding of the hurricane cone persists, highlighting a potentially dangerous gap between accurate forecasts and public preparedness.

more.title: Scientists discover a bizarre Jurassic “squid” unlike anything ever seen
more.summary: Scientists have identified the “fattest” belemnite ever discovered, a bizarre, barrel-shaped squid relative that lived in Wyoming’s ancient seas 160 million years ago. The exceptionally rare fossils reveal a creature unlike anything previously known, potentially a predator of smaller squid-like animals and a surprising survivor of a supposedly vanished family.

more.title: Shortening Canadian teacher education risks devaluing the profession of teaching
more.summary: Recently, shorter teacher certification programs have been introduced in different Canadian provinces. These programs are being implemented in Alberta, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Québec.

more.title: Where El Niño may impact California coastal areas this winter
more.summary: Driving across Highway 37 in the San Francisco Bay Area on the best of days already feels like driving on top of water. Buffeted on both sides by marshlands hosting egrets, herons, ducks and a handful of endangered species, the sea-level highway is a major connector linking Marin, Sonoma, Napa and Solano counties.

more.title: Shipwrecks can become thriving reefs, but may contain hidden toxic time bombs
more.summary: Late last year, scientists in Germany published findings on a World War II munitions dump in the Baltic Sea. Some may dismiss the dump as hazardous waste, but to marine biologists it was something far more exciting: a thriving ecosystem.

more.title: Building wildfire-resilient homes costs less than residents expect
more.summary: Housing development in Colorado is spreading into fire-prone landscapes, increasing wildfire risk and adding to the challenges of affordable housing and rising insurance costs.

more.title: Judging faces without personality labels uncovers key patterns in first impressions
more.summary: Imagine sitting on a city bus full of strangers. Look around at the people riding with you. If you needed help, how would you choose whom to trust? By scanning people's faces, your brain is already making interpretations about their personalities by judging certain facial features.

more.title: Mystery skeleton found in Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally have an identity
more.summary: The identity of a mysterious skeleton found in a Roman sarcophagus in the grounds of Westminster Abbey more than 150 years ago appears closer to being solved.

more.title: Northern Australia is a 'lifeboat' for critically endangered green sawfish
more.summary: Green sawfish, distinguished by their long, sharklike bodies and tooth-lined "saw" on the front of their heads, are on the verge of extinction, largely due to overfishing and habitat loss.

more.title: Caribbean islands were once the center of diversity for barn owls
more.summary: Legend has it that a giant elfin, owl-like creature called the chickcharney haunts the islands of the Bahamas. Those who encounter this cryptid on cordial terms are said to be blessed with good luck. Those who disrespect the chickcharney, however, don't fare as well.

more.title: Male seahorse pouch proteins may help remove toxic waste from developing embryos
more.summary: Male seahorses, fishes that belong to the Syngnathidae family, show a distinctive reproductive strategy in which males carry developing embryos in a brood pouch. Their most distinctive feature is the brood pouch on the ventral side of the male fish, into which the female fish transfers her eggs.

more.title: Are transgender sports bans really about protecting women? Survey data tells a different story
more.summary: Relatively few transgender athletes participate in high school and collegiate sports. Still, since 2020, 27 states have passed laws banning them from participating in sports based on their gender identity.

more.title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
more.summary: With the U.S. midterms approaching, about one in five voters has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found.
